narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 53.1% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tips just above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year grades had the strongest influence. Placing in the 4th decile, noticeably below the average of accepted students (5.79), this performance signaled a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam and pushed the prediction toward failure.

Next, your family income bracket of upper-middle class also contributed toward rejection. While this is the most common bracket among accepted students (45.4%), the model interpreted your specific combination of background and academic record as increasing the likelihood of not passing.

Your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction. At 30, it sits well below the 37.18 average of accepted students, yet the model still saw this score as a mildly positive factor that slightly reduced the predicted chance of failure.

Taken together, the weaker third-year academic standing outweighed the modest lift from your LSAT, tipping the overall prediction above the acceptance threshold.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Improving in these areas would most effectively lower your predicted risk of failing the bar and improve your chances in future applications. (218 words)
